Little Japanese horseshoe bats exhibit a slow reproductive pace, yielding a single pup per litter [N_R_i = single pup per litter] and producing just one litter per year [F_R_i = one litter per year], the latter representing their maximum reproductive rate under optimal thermal conditions. This low fecundity is consistent with the pattern observed across many rhinolophid species, which typically invest heavily in a single offspring each breeding season. Newborns emerge at a modest birth mass of approximately 1.9 grams [Wwb = approximately 1.9 grams], a value extrapolated from growth trajectory data and reflective of the altricial state of neonates in this genus. This initial weight stands in marked contrast to the ultimate adult body mass that individuals eventually attain. The protracted period of development and parental care suggests that even modest differences in neonatal provisioning can have lasting consequences for juvenile survival.

Adults of Rhinolophus cornutus reach a maximum adult body mass of 7.5 grams [Wwi = 7.5 grams], a figure consistent with the species' position among the smaller representatives of its genus. This asymptotic mass is reached after a sustained period of somatic growth, and field studies indicate that body condition fluctuates seasonally in response to prey abundance and reproductive demands. When maintained at a stable core temperature of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C], captive individuals have been documented to achieve a maximum lifespan of 30 years [am = 30 years], based on comparative data from related Rhinolophus species in the AnAge database. This remarkable longevity, exceeding that of many similarly sized insectivorous mammals, is likely linked to the species' low metabolic rate and the energy-conserving benefits of daily torpor, which reduce oxidative stress over the long term.

Gestation in the little Japanese horseshoe bat lasts approximately 67 days [tg = approximately 67 days], a value drawn from studies of the closely related Rhinolophus hipposideros, and this extended period unfolds under a maternal body temperature of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C]. This relatively lengthy gestation, for a mammal of such small body size, probably reflects the energetic constraints imposed by a low metabolic rate and the need to allocate resources efficiently during embryogenesis. The single embryo undergoes organogenesis and foetal development within the uterine environment, emerging as a well-proportioned though still altricial neonate after this period of internal development. Following birth, the pup remains entirely dependent on maternal lactation for nourishment, and the transition to nutritional independence occurs at a fixed developmental interval.

The nursing period culminates in weaning at 35 days after birth [tx = 35 days after birth], once again at a body temperature of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C], a value comparable to that documented in Rhinolophus hipposideros. During this suckling phase, the juvenile grows rapidly on a diet of milk, doubling or tripling its birth mass before beginning the dietary transition to solid food. The cessation of lactation marks a critical milestone, as the young bat must then acquire the foraging skills necessary to capture airborne insect prey independently. Field observations suggest that maternal investment during the pre-weaning period is intense, with females returning to the roost multiple times nightly to nurse their single offspring, a behavior that is energetically costly but essential for ensuring the pup's survival through its first winter.

Sexual maturation in Rhinolophus cornutus occurs at markedly different ages between the sexes when maintained at 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C]. Females experience their first litter at 500 days after birth [tp = 500 days after birth], a prolonged delay that reflects the time required to attain full somatic size and develop the reproductive endocrine axis at a temperature of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C]. Males, in contrast, become reproductively capable somewhat earlier, with first reproduction documented at 471 days after birth [tp = 471 days after birth], a difference that may be linked to the lower energetic demands of spermatogenesis compared to the substantial investment required for gestation and lactation in females at a temperature of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C]. This pattern of later female maturity is common among bats and is thought to reduce the risk of first-time mothers breeding before they have accumulated adequate fat reserves. The extended interval to first reproduction underscores the slow life-history strategy of this species.
